vignette: Akua had always loved her job as a tutor, working with children to help them catch up on their studies. But since the night she was raped, everything about her work - and her life - felt tainted. The sound of children crying, which used to be just a normal part of her day, now sent her spiraling into anxiety. She would feel a wave of nausea wash over her, and suddenly she was back in that room, reliving the terror. As the memories came flooding back, Akua couldn't shake the feeling that she had somehow brought this on herself. "If only I hadn't gone out that night," she would tell herself, or "If only I had fought harder." This self-blame became a constant refrain in her mind, making it impossible for her to escape the memories of that night. The more she ruminated on what had happened, the more convinced she became that she was permanently damaged - that she would never be able to go back to being the person she used to be. Akua tried to avoid anything that might trigger these feelings, including situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful. She stopped going out with friends, stopped taking on new students, and even stopped leaving the house unless absolutely necessary. But no matter how hard she tried to hide, the memories were always there, lurking just beneath the surface. And when they did surface - in dreams, in flashbacks, or simply in her mind's eye - Akua felt like she was reliving that terror all over again. The worst part was that Akua couldn't seem to put what had happened into words. She would try to talk about it with her partner, but the words just wouldn't come. It was as if her brain had somehow cordoned off that night, refusing to let her confront it head-on. This inability to verbalize her experience only added to Akua's feelings of shame and guilt - after all, if she couldn't even talk about what had happened, how could she possibly expect to overcome it? As the months went by, Akua became more and more withdrawn. She stopped engaging with her partner, stopped participating in activities she used to love, and even stopped taking care of herself. It was as if she had given up - not just on herself, but on life itself. And yet, despite all this, Akua couldn't shake the feeling that she was somehow to blame for everything that had happened. One day, while out running errands, Akua saw a flyer for a support group for survivors of sexual assault. Something about it caught her eye - maybe it was the promise of being around others who understood what she was going through, or maybe it was just the desperation in her own heart. Whatever it was, Akua knew that she had to take action - not just for herself, but for the life she once knew and loved. Akua's partner encouraged her to seek help, pointing out that things couldn't keep going on like this. But Akua was terrified of what might happen if she started talking about her experiences - would she fall apart completely? Would she be unable to handle it? In the end, it was this fear that finally brought her to therapy - not a desire to "get better," per se, but a desperate hope that somehow, someway, she might be able to find a way out of this darkness and back into the light.
